steps.q: Why do process heaters use saturated steam rather than superheated steam?
steps.title: Why saturated?
steps.summary: Saturated steam heats by condensing on the surface, giving up its latent heat at a single fixed temperature with a very high film coefficient. Superheated steam must first cool like a gas, with poor heat transfer and uneven temperatures, so steam is usually desuperheated before process heaters and jackets.

steps.q: Why reduce steam from 10 barg to 3.5 barg for heating, if the process allows?
steps.title: Lower pressure
steps.summary: Steam at 10 barg condenses at about 184 °C and releases about 477 kcal/kg; at 3.5 barg it condenses at about 148 °C and releases about 506 kcal/kg. Lower-pressure steam gives more latent heat per kilogram, a gentler wall temperature and less flash steam, but the smaller temperature difference may need more heat transfer area.

steps.q: What does a steam trap do?
board: What does a steam trap do?
steps.title: The trap's job
steps.summary: A steam trap lets condensate and air out while holding steam in, so equipment does not flood and steam stays to give up its heat. Float traps suit heat exchangers with varying loads; thermodynamic traps suit steam main drains. Air must also be removed, because it blankets heat transfer surfaces and lowers the effective steam temperature.

steps.q: An open trap discharge shows a big white cloud. Has the trap failed?
steps.title: Flash or live?
steps.summary: When hot condensate drops to atmospheric pressure, part of it flashes to steam, forming a lazy white cloud, which is normal. Live steam blowing through a failed-open trap shows as a fast, nearly clear jet at the outlet that turns white further away. Stand clear of the outlet, since live steam near it is invisible and burns, and confirm with an ultrasonic check; a trap failed open wastes steam continuously.

opts.t: Yes, if the cloud is big

draw: stand clear: live steam is invisible

steps.q: Condensate at 7 barg is let down to atmosphere. Roughly what share flashes to steam?
steps.title: Flash steam
steps.summary: Condensate at 7 barg is at about 170 °C and holds about 172 kcal/kg. At atmospheric pressure water can hold only about 100 kcal/kg, so the extra 72 kcal/kg evaporates part of it; at about 539 kcal/kg latent heat, that is 72 ÷ 539 ≈ 13 %. Flash steam can be recovered in a flash vessel for low-pressure heating.

steps.q: Steam mains bang loudly when steam is let in at start-up. What is the main cause?
board: when steam is let in at
steps.title: Drain the mains
steps.summary: When steam enters a cold main, condensate forms and collects at low points. Fast steam picks it up into slugs that strike bends with great force: water hammer. Fit drip legs with traps at every low point and every 30 to 50 m on long runs, and warm mains up slowly with the drains open.

opts.t: The boiler pressure is too high

draw: drip leg + trap at low points,

intro.text: Hi, I'm Bubbles. Today: steam, the plant's favourite way to move heat, and the traps that keep it honest. Six questions. Ready?

outro-web.text: That's the lesson. Now try the steam heating calculator.

q1.text: Question 1. Why do process heaters use saturated steam rather than superheated steam?

q1-r0.text: Hotter, yes. Better for heating, no. It gives its heat up slowly.

q1-r1.text: Yes! Latent heat, at one steady temperature.

q1-r2.text: It's a little cheaper, but that's not the main reason.

q1-r3.text: It flows just fine. Turbines love it.

q1-b0.text: Saturated steam condenses on the tube wall and gives up its latent heat at one fixed temperature.

q1-b1.text: Condensing gives a very high film coefficient. Much higher than a gas cooling down.

q1-b2.text: Superheated steam has to cool down like a gas first. Poor heat transfer, and uneven temperatures.

q1-b3.text: So plants desuperheat steam before it reaches heaters and jackets.

q2.text: Question 2. Why reduce steam from 10 barg to 3.5 barg for heating, if the process allows?

q2-r0.text: The boiler makes it at one pressure anyway. Look at the heat per kilo.

q2-r1.text: Correct! More useful heat per kilo, and gentler on the product.

q2-r2.text: It condenses fine, just at a higher temperature.

q2-b0.text: At 10 bar gauge, steam condenses at about 184 degrees and gives about 477 kilocalories per kilogram.

q2-b1.text: At 3.5 bar gauge, it condenses at about 148 degrees and gives about 506.

q2-b2.text: So each kilogram gives more heat, the product sees a gentler wall, and less flashes off from the condensate.

q2-b3.text: The catch: lower pressure means a smaller temperature difference, so you may need more area.

q3.text: Question 3. What does a steam trap do?

q3-r0.text: Exactly backwards. That would flood your heater.

q3-r1.text: Yes! Water out, steam stays to do its job.

q3-r2.text: A trap doesn't add pressure. It just sorts water from steam.

q3-b0.text: Steam condenses as it gives up heat. That condensate has to leave, or it floods the equipment.

q3-b1.text: A trap opens for condensate and air, and closes against steam.

q3-b2.text: Float traps, with a built-in air vent, suit heat exchangers with changing loads. Thermodynamic traps suit steam main drains.

q3-b3.text: Air must go too. It blankets the surface and lowers the steam temperature.

q4.text: Question 4. An open trap discharge shows a big white cloud. Has the trap failed?

q4-r0.text: Not always. Some of that cloud is meant to be there.

q4-r1.text: Right! Hot condensate flashes when the pressure drops.

q4-r2.text: Cloud size mostly tracks load and pressure. Look at the jet.

q4-r3.text: Noise alone won't tell you. Look at the jet.

q4-b0.text: Condensate at steam temperature drops to atmospheric pressure. Part of it boils off as flash steam.

q4-b1.text: Flash steam is a lazy, white cloud that drifts up from the condensate.

q4-b2.text: Live steam blowing through a failed trap is a fast, almost clear jet right at the outlet, then turns white further out.

q4-b3.text: Stand clear of the outlet: near it, live steam is invisible and burns. Confirm with an ultrasonic check. A trap failed open wastes steam every hour of the year.

q5.text: Question 5. Condensate at 7 barg is let down to atmosphere. Roughly what share flashes to steam?

q5-r0.text: Much more than that. The condensate is very hot.

q5-r2.text: Half? That's a lot more than the heat available.

q5-r3.text: None? Then where does that white cloud come from?

q5-b0.text: Condensate at 7 bar gauge is at about 170 degrees, holding about 172 kilocalories per kilogram.

q5-b1.text: At atmospheric pressure, water can only hold 100 kilocalories per kilogram. The extra 72 boils some of it off.

q5-b2.text: Each kilogram boiled takes about 539 kilocalories. 72 over 539 is about 13 percent.

q5-b3.text: That flash steam is real energy. Recover it in a flash vessel for low-pressure heating.

q6.text: Question 6. Steam mains bang loudly when steam is let in at start-up. What is the main cause?

q6-r0.text: Dry steam is what you want. Something wet is the problem.

q6-r1.text: High pressure alone doesn't bang. Water does.

q6-r2.text: Yes! Water slugs hit the bends. That's water hammer.

q6-r3.text: A big pipe isn't the reason for the bang.

q6-b0.text: A cold main fills with condensate as steam warms it. That water collects at low points.

q6-b1.text: Steam rushing in picks the water up into a slug and hurls it at the next bend. Bang.

q6-b2.text: Fit drip legs with traps at every low point and every 30 to 50 metres on long runs.

q6-b3.text: And warm mains up slowly, with drains open. Check your loads in the steam heating calculator on pharmacheme dot in.
